description: Essex's rebellion, monopolies and the succession question in Elizabeth's final decade.
content_html:
The Final Years: Decline and Challenges

The last decade of Elizabeth’s reign (1593–1603) stands in stark contrast to the triumphalism of the Armada’s defeat. An expensive war in Ireland, the continuing conflict with Spain, harvest failures in the 1590s, rising prices, tensions at court and an aging Queen who refused to name a successor all combined to create a mood of uncertainty and frustration. The Elizabethan political system, which had worked brilliantly when Elizabeth was energetic and in command, began to show its weaknesses as the Queen grew old and her early advisers died.

The Death of Lord Burghley, 1598

The death of Lord Burghley in August 1598 was a significant moment. Cecil had been the linchpin of Elizabethan government for almost forty years. His cautious, pragmatic approach had steered England through the most dangerous moments of the reign. His son Robert Cecil stepped into his administrative role and served as Secretary of State from 1596, but the dynamic of the court changed. Without Burghley’s steady hand, factional rivalry between Robert Cecil’s cautious group and the more aggressive faction surrounding the Earl of Essex intensified.

Monopolies were royal licences granting exclusive rights to produce or sell a particular product — salt, starch, playing cards, vinegar and many others. Elizabeth used them extensively to reward favourites and raise money without parliamentary taxation. By the 1590s, however, the system had become deeply unpopular: monopolies raised prices for consumers and restricted trade. MPs in the Parliament of 1601 complained bitterly, and an MP reportedly asked whether bread itself would be monopolised. Elizabeth responded with her characteristic skill: rather than defending the system, she withdrew the worst monopolies before Parliament could force a confrontation, and met a delegation of MPs herself to express sympathy with their grievances. This episode became known as the ‘Golden Speech’ of 1601, in which she reportedly expressed her deep love for her people and her gratitude for their loyalty.

Key Fact

The monopolies crisis of 1601 showed both Elizabeth’s political skill and the growing frustrations of her later reign. She defused the confrontation by withdrawing the most unpopular monopolies before Parliament could force a legal challenge — a tactful retreat that was publicly presented as royal generosity rather than defeat.

The Essex Rebellion, 1601

Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex, was the last of Elizabeth’s great court favourites. He was young, dashing and ambitious — the son-in-law of Francis Walsingham — and Elizabeth had shown him exceptional favour, granting him military commands and a lucrative licence on sweet wines. But Essex was erratic and prone to rage; he had publicly quarrelled with Elizabeth to her face on at least one occasion. In 1599 he was appointed Lord Lieutenant of Ireland to crush the rebellion led by Hugh O’Neill, Earl of Tyrone. Instead, he negotiated an unauthorised truce with Tyrone, returned to England without permission and burst into Elizabeth’s private chambers to justify himself.

Stripped of his offices and his wine licence (which was his main source of income), Essex grew increasingly desperate. On 8 February 1601 he rode through the streets of London with around 200 followers, calling on the citizens to rise against his enemies at court — whom he accused of being traitors advising the Queen poorly. The citizens did not rise; Essex’s coup collapsed almost immediately. He was arrested, tried for treason and executed on 25 February 1601. Elizabeth reportedly wept when she signed his death warrant. The rebellion exposed the dangerous personal dependencies that the Elizabethan court system had created — favourites could become liabilities when favour was withdrawn.

Key Fact

Essex’s failure in Ireland (1599) — making an unauthorised truce with Tyrone and returning without permission — and his subsequent loss of court favour led directly to his rebellion of February 1601. He was executed on 25 February 1601 after his attempt to raise London against his enemies at court collapsed immediately.

The Succession Question

Throughout her reign Elizabeth refused to name a successor, believing that naming an heir would create a focus for opposition and destabilise her own position. The succession question became acute in her final years as it became clear she would never marry. James VI of Scotland, the Protestant son of Mary Queen of Scots, was the strongest claimant. Robert Cecil had secretly been corresponding with James for months before Elizabeth’s death to ensure a smooth transition.

Elizabeth I died on 24 March 1603 at Richmond Palace, aged sixty-nine, after several weeks of declining health. She had been Queen for forty-four years. Within hours of her death, Robert Cecil publicly proclaimed James VI of Scotland as James I of England. The transition was peaceful — the succession problem Elizabeth had refused to resolve for forty years was resolved almost instantaneously after her death.

Elizabeth’s legacy is genuinely complex. On one reading, she was an extraordinarily successful monarch who presided over a religious settlement that brought stability, who defeated the Spanish Armada, who oversaw the flowering of English literature and theatre, and who ruled for forty-four years in a period when female rule was deeply suspect. On another reading, she left serious problems unresolved: the succession was uncertain until the moment of her death; the war with Spain was still dragging on; the Church settlement pleased no one fully; poverty and vagrancy were worse at the end of her reign than the beginning; and her refusal to invest in Ireland left a festering conflict that would trouble her successors for decades. Judgement depends on what you prioritise — stability and survival, or resolution of underlying problems.
exam_tip_html: Questions about the end of Elizabeth’s reign often appear as ‘How far did Elizabeth maintain control of her government?’ or as part of broader essays on her success. For these, use the Essex rebellion (1601) and the monopolies crisis (1601) as concrete examples of challenges — but also show Elizabeth’s skill in resolving them: Essex was executed cleanly; the monopolies crisis was defused by the Golden Speech. For 16-mark period essays asking how far Elizabeth was a successful ruler, you need evidence from across the whole reign (early, middle and late) and must address what ‘success’ means before reaching a substantiated judgement.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The final decade was marked by challenges: Burghley’s death (1598) left a power vacuum; the monopolies crisis (1601) provoked serious parliamentary opposition, defused by Elizabeth’s ‘Golden Speech’; and the Essex Rebellion (February 1601) was a direct but short-lived challenge, crushed by Essex’s execution on 25 February 1601.
  • Elizabeth refused to name a successor throughout her reign. Robert Cecil secretly prepared James VI of Scotland’s accession; within hours of Elizabeth’s death on 24 March 1603 James was proclaimed king, and the transition was peaceful.
  • Elizabeth’s legacy is debated: achievements (stability, the Armada, cultural flowering) must be weighed against unresolved problems (succession, poverty, Ireland, incomplete religious settlement). Historians disagree on how far her reign was a genuine ‘Golden Age.’

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Essex Rebellion of 1601.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: a precise feature with detail, e.g. the Earl of Essex rode through London on 8 February 1601 with around 200 followers calling on citizens to rise against his enemies at court, but the citizens did not respond (2 marks). Emerging: a vague feature (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the monopolies crisis of 1601.
practice_questions.marks: For each feature: Mastering: precise feature with accurate detail (2 marks). Emerging: simple feature without development (1 mark). Features may include: monopolies were royal licences giving exclusive trading rights; they had raised prices and restricted trade; MPs complained bitterly in the 1601 Parliament; Elizabeth defused the crisis by withdrawing the worst monopolies before Parliament could force a confrontation; the 'Golden Speech' expressed her love for her people. Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Earl of Essex's failure in Ireland (1599) for his position at court.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: detailed causal chain with evidence, e.g. Essex's unauthorised truce with Tyrone and return to England without permission led to his loss of offices and his wine licence — his main income; stripped of influence and income, and fearing the growing power of Robert Cecil, Essex turned to rebellion as his only remaining option. Secure: clear consequence with some evidence. Developing: relevant consequence with limited development. Emerging: simple point. Maximum 6 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the death of William Cecil, Lord Burghley, in 1598 for the government of Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained analysis of significance at the time (loss of his steadying pragmatic influence; intensified court factionalism; power vacuum partly filled by Robert Cecil, but without the same authority) AND over time (the factional tensions contributed directly to the Essex rebellion and the political turbulence of Elizabeth's final years). Secure: clear explanation with specific evidence. Developing: some explanation. Emerging: simple points. Maximum 8 marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful is the account of a courtier present in London during the Essex Rebellion of 1601 for understanding why it failed so quickly?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: integrates content (what the courtier describes), provenance (a court insider — may present a loyalist perspective; an eyewitness but with limited view) and contextual knowledge (the citizens did not rise; Essex's support was narrow; he was quickly arrested) to give a substantiated judgement on utility and limitations. Secure: addresses two elements. Developing: mainly describes source. Emerging: simple comment. Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: 'Elizabeth I's authority was weaker at the end of her reign (1593–1603) than it had been in her earlier years.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: argues for (Essex Rebellion; monopolies crisis; loss of key advisers; Irish failure; financial strain; no named successor) AND against (Essex rebellion was crushed swiftly; monopolies crisis was defused; Robert Cecil managed succession seamlessly; the settlement survived; no major foreign threat after the Armada) before a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: both sides with evidence and conclusion. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: simple. Maximum 12 marks.

knowledge_checks.q: On what date was the Earl of Essex executed following his failed rebellion?
Why did Elizabeth's 'Golden Speech' in 1601 help to defuse the monopolies crisis?
options: She promised to abolish all taxation for five years
She publicly withdrew the most unpopular monopolies before Parliament could force a legal challenge
She agreed to summon Parliament every year from 1602 onwards
She granted MPs the right to approve all future monopolies

knowledge_checks.q: Elizabeth I died on 24 March _____ at Richmond Palace, aged sixty-nine.
The man who secretly prepared James VI of Scotland's peaceful accession to the English throne was Robert _____.
Match each event of Elizabeth I's final decade to its correct year:

flashcard_questions.q: When did Lord Burghley die and why was his death significant?
flashcard_questions.a: August 1598; he had been Elizabeth's principal adviser for nearly forty years and his death intensified court factionalism.

flashcard_questions.q: What were monopolies and why did they become controversial?
flashcard_questions.a: Royal licences granting exclusive trading rights; they raised prices and restricted trade, causing serious public anger.

flashcard_questions.q: How did Elizabeth defuse the monopolies crisis in 1601?
flashcard_questions.a: She withdrew the most unpopular monopolies before Parliament could force a confrontation, presenting it as royal generosity.

flashcard_questions.q: Who was the Earl of Essex?
flashcard_questions.a: Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex — the last of Elizabeth's great favourites, executed for rebellion in 1601.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did Essex's rebellion on 8 February 1601 fail so quickly?
flashcard_questions.a: London's citizens did not rise in support; Essex had only around 200 followers and was swiftly arrested.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did Elizabeth refuse to name a successor throughout her reign?
flashcard_questions.a: She believed naming an heir would create a focus for opposition and destabilise her own position.

flashcard_questions.q: Who succeeded Elizabeth I and when?
flashcard_questions.a: James VI of Scotland, proclaimed James I of England on 24 March 1603, hours after Elizabeth's death.

flashcard_questions.q: What was Elizabeth I's 'Golden Speech' of 1601?
flashcard_questions.a: A speech expressing deep love for her people, delivered when defusing the monopolies crisis in Parliament.

flashcard_questions.q: What unresolved problem did Elizabeth leave for her successors in Ireland?
flashcard_questions.a: An ongoing rebellion led by Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone, which Essex had failed to crush.

flashcard_questions.q: How long was Elizabeth I's reign?
flashcard_questions.a: Forty-four years, from November 1558 to March 1603.

glossary_terms.definition: William Cecil, Elizabeth's most trusted adviser for nearly forty years, whose death in August 1598 left a power vacuum at court.
Royal licences granting individuals the exclusive right to produce or sell a particular commodity, used by Elizabeth to reward favourites but bitterly resented by 1601.
Robert Devereux, a court favourite of Elizabeth I who led a disastrous Irish campaign and was executed for attempted rebellion in February 1601.
The Protestant son of Mary Queen of Scots who succeeded Elizabeth I as James I of England in March 1603, beginning the Stuart dynasty.
